$comment: Rules for scripts/check-open-boundary.mjs — the pre-open CONTENT + DEPENDENCY
audits (docs/explanation/OPEN_SOURCE_STRATEGY.md, 'Pre-open checklist' →
Content audit, Dependency audit), executed as a gate over the working tree.
Companion to scripts/history-scan.rules.json, which asks the same questions of
HISTORY. The path rules here are deliberately the same rules, with the same ids
and the same patterns, and tests/open_boundary_selftest.mjs asserts that they
have not drifted apart: a rule that fires on a blob but not on the file it came
from (or the reverse) is a gate somebody will point at and be wrong about.
Rule kinds:
contentRules       — path patterns for content that must not be vendored into
an open repo. `remove` means it must never appear;
`review` means a human classifies each hit in `allow`.
buildFetchRules    — line patterns for a build that reaches the network. In a
CMake/C tree this is the dependency audit's other half:
a dependency the build DOWNLOADS is a dependency nobody
declared, and it is not covered by any import graph.
closedRepoPackages — the CLOSED repos by package/crate name. A named
deny-list, for a better error message than the general
rule gives.
runtimeBackEdges   — packages that violate the one-way rule: runtimes depend
on core, never the reverse; and libinsimul is layer zero
under all of them.
allowedCrates      — every registry crate any shipped Rust artifact may
depend on, each one read and classified by a human.
Neither deny-list is load-bearing. What closes the graph is that the general
rules leave nothing unaccounted for: `undeclared-dependency` (this repository
declares NO npm dependencies, so every bare JS specifier is a finding),
`undeclared-crate` (every registry crate must be on the list below),
`escaping-c-include` / `absolute-path-import` (no #include leaves the tree), and
`build-time-fetch` (the build downloads nothing, so the bytes compiled are the
bytes committed). A deny-list catches the import somebody writes on purpose;
those catch the one nobody thought of, including a closed package renamed
tomorrow.
There is deliberately NO rule that matches closed generation tables by value. A
deny-list of the real numbers would have to contain the real numbers, in the
open repository, which is the leak it is meant to prevent wearing a guard's
clothes. The structural detector shared with check-pack-provenance.mjs is what
stands in for it; that file's header argues the point at length.
`allow` is where the human decisions live. A finding with no allowance fails
the gate — the scanner reports, it does not decide. An allowance that matches
nothing also fails the gate: a stale allowance is a hole nobody is watching.
An entry keys on `path` or on `pathPrefix` (this repository's addition, as in
history-scan.rules.json: 39 vendored engine .pl files and one committed
benchmark world stay VISIBLE in the report instead of disappearing into a rule
`except`), and on `specifier` when it names one.
Patterns are JavaScript regular expressions. A contentRule's is matched against
the repo-relative, forward-slashed path; a buildFetchRule's against each line
of the file, comment-only lines excepted. A leading `(?i)` becomes the `i` flag.
$declaredNpmDependencies: EMPTY, and that is the point. This repository has no package.json and installs
nothing from npm: the wasm package.json is GENERATED by scripts/package.sh with
empty dependencies on purpose (the dependency direction is one-way, nothing here
may depend on a JS consumer), and every .mjs in the tree runs on a bare node.
So the rule core states as 'a builtin or a declared dependency' reads here as
'a Node builtin, full stop' — stricter than core's, not weaker.

contentRules.description: The closed genre/language world packs and generation heuristics (data/insimul/**, OPEN_SOURCE_STRATEGY.md 'The content boundary'). These are the CLOSED asset and must never be vendored into an open repo. This repository has never had one; the rule is the guard that says so, and it stays whether or not it fires.

native-specific. A directory of world/pack content. libinsimul is the ENGINE — the thing that runs a world — and a world committed into it is either a fixture (fine, and classified as one) or a piece of the closed authoring content that must never be here. `bench/world/` is the committed benchmark fixture and is classified in `allow`; anything else that lands under this pattern needs a human before the flip.

A .pl source. The Prolog ENGINE is open and contract-level base predicates ship — they must, for conformance — but the genre bundles, the language corpora (CEFR/SRS data, the ~573 .pl seed files) and the generation heuristics do not. Every .pl in the tree is therefore classified by hand; a NEW one fails this gate until somebody writes down which side of the line it is on. The closed asset and the open asset have the same file extension, so the extension cannot decide.

A signed/licensed pack bundle by extension. Packs ship signed and licensed and are never committed to a repo that is or will be public — including inside an archive whose contents this scan cannot read.

native-specific. A compiled or packaged artifact by extension. Two reasons it is a finding rather than a nuisance: this repository BUILDS wasm modules, preload images, static libraries and dist tarballs, so a committed one is a real possibility; and no scanner here can read one, so a binary in the tree is a hole in the audit that a human has to close by knowing what it is. `.data` is Emscripten's preload image — the one artifact here that can carry a whole Prolog library tree inside it.

native-specific. A build or dependency tree that .gitignore is supposed to keep out (build/, build-wasm/, dist/, node_modules/, rust's target/). Committed build output is how a binary — engine objects, a preload image, a packaged shared library — reaches a repository that reads as pure source.

buildFetchRules.description: A build step that reaches the network. libinsimul is layer zero — four engine runtimes, the Rust server and every save file sit on it — so what it compiles must be what is committed (see CLAUDE.md, 'The engine source is VENDORED here'). A fetched input is a dependency the import graph cannot see, cannot pin and cannot audit, and it is how a repository that reads as self-contained stops being so. Every hit is classified by hand: the DEFAULT build (CMakeLists.txt, cmake/**) must have none at all.

closedRepoPackages.reason: insimul-backend is CLOSED — generators, ToT/Kismet simulation, LLM pipelines, export/IR, auth, jobs. It is the moat (OPEN_SOURCE_STRATEGY.md, 'Open / Closed by repo'), and the checklist calls backend extraction a hard wall: no generator or pipeline code reachable from an open repo.
Same repo, as a Rust crate name.
insimul-web is CLOSED — the React editor client and the primary product surface, which integrates into the commercial Studio OS layer.
Same repo, as a Rust crate name.
The closed platform tree (server, pipelines, editor client). Named separately because the split moved code out of it and a leftover specifier is the likeliest form of the mistake.
Generation pipelines — the closed half of the content boundary.

runtimeBackEdges.reason: A `@shared/*` specifier names no package: it is a tsconfig alias whose modules re-export into a runtime AND into the closed platform. It is the sneaky form of the back-edge — it satisfies a compiler that has the alias and resolves to nothing in a standalone clone. Nothing here has such an alias, so anything matching this is a copied line, not a working import.
The Babylon runtime. libinsimul is layer ZERO: runtimes depend on it, it depends on no runtime. The same one-way rule core states, one layer down.
The Babylon game shell. Same one-way rule.
An engine runtime repo. Same one-way rule — insimul-godot consumes insimulcore.h from here, never the reverse.
A rendering engine. This library owns no scene graph and no DOM.
This is a C library with a wasm build; nothing here has a DOM.

allowedCrates.reason: Traits only — rust/insimul/src/term.rs writes its Deserialize by hand (no derive) so the binding-set map keeps the ABI's variable order, which is part of the contract include/insimul.h promises. Dual MIT/Apache-2.0, so it is compatible with this repository's licence either way; pure-Rust, no build-time network, no transitive path into any closed repo (its only dependency is serde_core/serde_derive from the same crate family).

Parses the binding-set JSON the bootstrap emits ('$ij_esc'/2, RFC 8259, lossless). Dual MIT/Apache-2.0; depends on serde, itoa, ryu, memchr — all from the same maintainer set and all pure Rust. It is a JSON parser: it opens no socket, spawns no process, and reaches nothing.

$comment: Prefixes an open tree's pack ids may declare, passed to the same detector
check-pack-provenance.mjs and the US-1 history scan use — `probe/` for VM
probes, `test.` for unit fixtures, `example/` for documentation. A closed
pack is named for the product it belongs to, so renaming one to get past
this is not a slip anybody makes by accident.

allow.reason: The vendored Prolog ENGINE's own standard library (39 files: lists, assoc, dcgs, clpz, format, …), not authoring content. It is upstream Trealla's `library/` directory at the pinned commit 07de013677af760a8bca0594ae4b2bef158a3cde, licensed BSD-2-Clause (docs/TREALLA_LICENSE_FINDING.md §4), and the bytes on disk are PROVEN to be upstream's by tests/run_trealla_vendor.sh, which recomputes git's own tree/blob ids for every vendored path offline. So this is not a judgement about 39 files nobody read: it is a judgement about one pinned upstream directory whose identity is already a ctest. Same decision as the US-1 history audit's finding 1.

The ABI bootstrap — the Prolog that IS libinsimul's C layer (running goals, serialising the binding-set JSON, classifying ISO errors, snapshotting). Every promise include/insimul.h makes is implemented here. It is engine plumbing and the open half of the content boundary by definition: a runtime cannot be shown conformant against an ABI whose implementation it cannot read. No genre bundle, no language corpus, no generation heuristic.

The golden snapshot image the `snapshot_parse` ctest parses with the wrappers' real prolog-fact-parser.ts. Six clauses of throwaway fixture data (parent/2, likes/2) chosen to exercise quoting and variable rendering. Contract-level by construction: the file exists to pin the snapshot FORMAT, which is part of what a swapped engine must reproduce byte for byte.

The committed benchmark world (6 .pl files, 1,630 clauses) that scripts/measure.sh times both engines against. It is not authoring content and it is not hand-curated: bench/world/generate.mjs produces every byte deterministically from a fixed LCG with no clock, and `generate.mjs --check` re-derives and compares them before any figure is measured. So the closed asset it could be mistaken for — a curated world, a generation heuristic — is precisely what its own generator proves it is not. Same decision as the US-1 history audit's finding 4.

The same 10 files, caught a second time by the directory-shaped rule rather than the extension-shaped one (the generator, its MANIFEST.json, QUERIES.txt and README.md alongside the six .pl). Both rules are kept and both fire on purpose: one asks 'is this .pl authoring content', the other asks 'is there a world tree in the ENGINE repo', and a leak that dodges one should still hit the other.

A BUNDLE INPUT, not a runtime import. corebridge/js/entry.js is the adapter esbuild reads when corebridge/tools/vendor-core-bundle.mjs re-vendors the core bundle; the specifier is resolved then, against a sibling @insimul/core checkout the vendoring tool is pointed at, and the artifact that ships (corebridge/vendor/core/insimul-core-bundle.js) carries ZERO bare specifiers — it is a closed graph, which this same scan verifies by reading it like any other file. @insimul/core is an OPEN repo (OPEN_SOURCE_STRATEGY.md names it the first to open), so the edge is open→open even at vendor time, and it is the dependency direction the README already describes: runtimes consume core.

As above — the contract-level radiant base templates, resolved at bundle time from the open core package. The allowance is per-SPECIFIER rather than per-file on purpose: a path-only allowance would silently bless every future bare import anybody adds to this file, which is the one place in the tree where adding one is easy.

As above. `@insimul/core-scripts` is not a published package: it is an alias vendor-core-bundle.mjs maps onto core's own scripts/ directory so the golden-manifest helper can be bundled from the same checkout. Open→open, resolved at vendor time, absent from the shipped artifact.

THE FINDING THAT PROVES THE FIXTURE IS SAFE. The gate's own self-test has no basename exemption (see check-open-boundary.mjs's divergence 4), so it is audited like every other file — and what the scanner reads at these lines is the literal text `${CLOSED_BACKEND}`, a template placeholder, because the forbidden specifier is assembled by concatenation at run time and appears nowhere in the file's bytes. That is why the finding is `undeclared-dependency` and not `closed-repo-import`: had the fixture contained the real string, this entry would be the wrong rule and the gate would say so. A placeholder resolves to nothing and imports nothing; the file is a test that never runs its own fixtures as code.
As above — the same placeholder, in the fixture that exercises the require() form.
As above — the same placeholder with a subpath, in the fixture that exercises a deep import.

The negative control's payload: this is the driver that injects a FetchContent declaration into a THROWAWAY copy of the tree to prove this very rule can fail. Same argument as tests/run_trealla_vendor.sh's entry — deleting the line to satisfy the rule would delete the proof that the rule works. It fetches nothing itself; the string is an argument to printf.

The ONE fetch in the tree that builds anything, and it is opt-in: this script clones upstream SWI-Prolog at its pin and installs it to a prefix, for the `-DINSIMUL_ENGINE=swipl` spike only. It is never invoked by `cmake --build`, the default engine is the VENDORED Trealla, and D20 (docs/SWIPL_MEASUREMENT.md) answered the spike NO — chief/252 stays parked. SWI is located, not vendored (CLAUDE.md, 'Two engines, one tree'), so nothing it downloads is committed here or shipped; cmake/swipl.cmake refuses a prefix that does not carry the pin file this script writes. Named rather than hidden because the shape is a real risk: a spike helper is exactly how a fetch becomes load-bearing later.

Two `git clone`s of THIS repository — the mirror-and-rewrite dance the prepared history rewrite would run at flip time (US-1). It compiles nothing, is human-gated, refuses --execute while the plan purges nothing, and the thing it clones is the repository itself.

Two `git clone`s of a throwaway repository the gate itself creates under mktemp -d, to run a real git filter-repo over a planted secret (check D). Both operands are local paths in the same temp directory; no network is involved and nothing is compiled.

This is the rule's ally, not its violator: run_trealla_vendor.sh is the gate that FAILS the build if the engine is ever fetched instead of vendored, and the three hits are its own machinery — declares_fetch(), and the deliberately broken fixture declaring FetchContent from example.invalid that proves the check can fail. Deleting these lines to satisfy a fetch rule would delete the check that enforces it.
